name: Pécs
tagline: A sunny southern city with Roman tombs, a mosque-turned-church, a four-towered cathedral and the colourful Zsolnay ceramic quarter.
highlight: The Mosque-Church on Széchenyi Square, a domed Ottoman mosque topped with a cross.
shortDescription: A Mediterranean-feeling city with early Christian tombs, the Gazi Kasim Pasha Mosque, a four-towered cathedral, Zsolnay ceramics and nearby Villány red wines.
metaDescription: A Pécs travel guide: the Mosque-Church, Early Christian Necropolis, the Cathedral, Zsolnay Quarter, Villány wine, how to get there from Budapest and a two-day plan.
nearestAirport: Budapest Ferenc Liszt (BUD), about 3–4 hours by road or train

intro: Pécs is a city of about 140,000 people at the foot of the Mecsek hills in southern Hungary, and it has one of the mildest climates in the country. It has been settled since Roman times, when it was called Sopianae, and its layers of history are unusually visible: Roman-era Christian tombs, a medieval cathedral, an Ottoman mosque, and Art Nouveau ceramics from the Zsolnay factory.

The most famous building is the Mosque-Church of Pasha Gazi Kasim on Széchenyi Square, built in the 16th century during the Ottoman occupation and later converted into a Catholic church, with Islamic prayer niche and Christian symbols side by side. Nearby, the four-towered cathedral is a neo-Romanesque giant, and the Early Christian Necropolis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contains painted burial chambers from the 4th century.

The Zsolnay Cultural Quarter celebrates the local porcelain, with its shimmering eosin-glazed tiles visible on rooftops across the city. Pécs was European Capital of Culture in 2010, and has good cafés, museums and a warm, unhurried feel. To the south, the Villány wine region produces some of Hungary's best reds. Two days is ideal.

whyVisit.intro: Pécs is a layered, sunny city with a fine cultural life and few tourists.
